claim_checks.claim: `private` and `protected` are enforced only during type checking. Runtime lookups, and bracket notation even during type checking, still reach the member: it is "soft private".
claim_checks.page_says: private and protected are only enforced during type checking. ... private also allows access using bracket notation during type checking. ... these fields are soft private
claim_checks.note: The handbook supports runtime lookups for both private and protected members, but it states the bracket-notation escape hatch and the 'soft private' label for private only. 'The member' in the claim covers protected as well, which is a wider scope than the page.

claim_checks.claim: `#` fields stay private after compilation and have no bracket-notation escape hatch: they are "hard private".
claim_checks.page_says: JavaScript’s private fields (#) remain private after compilation and do not provide the previously mentioned escape hatches like bracket notation access, making them hard private.

claim_checks.claim: When compiling to ES2021 or lower, TypeScript replaces `#` with `WeakMap`s. The handbook notes that these runtime privacy checks could affect performance.
claim_checks.page_says: When compiling to ES2021 or less, TypeScript will use WeakMaps in place of #. ... Note that these added privacy checks during runtime could affect performance.
claim_checks.note: Both parts are on the page, with 'could' kept. The handbook's caution covers closures, WeakMaps and native private fields alike; the claim applies it to the WeakMap case only, which is narrower and still supported (see conflicts).

claim_checks.claim: Private elements are not properties. They cannot be enumerated, deleted, proxied, or reached through `Object` methods, and `structuredClone()` does not copy them.
claim_checks.page_says: they cannot be proxied, enumerated, deleted, or interacted with using any Object method. ... structuredClone() does not clone private elements
claim_checks.note: 'Not properties' matches MDN's note that a property has a string or symbol key and attributes, which private elements lack.

claim_checks.claim: Reading a `#` field from an object whose class did not declare it throws a `TypeError`. `#x in obj` checks for it without throwing.
claim_checks.page_says: Cannot read private member #x from an object whose class did not declare it ... use the in operator to check whether an externally defined object possesses a private element
claim_checks.note: MDN states the TypeError rule and shows this exact message; the in check returns true or false, and its example passes {} without an error.

claim_checks.claim: V8 9.7 moved class-field initialization, including private fields, onto its inline-cache fast path. Before that it went through slower runtime calls.
claim_checks.page_says: Before v9.7, V8 always used a costly runtime call ... With v9.7, when V8 considers the pattern of the initialization to be predictable enough, it uses a new IC
claim_checks.note: The version and the runtime-call history are supported. The page makes the fast path conditional (pattern predictable enough) and says initialization falls back to a runtime call otherwise, for example on proxies or unseen hidden classes. The claim drops that condition.

claim_checks.claim: Private elements cannot be proxied (row context: Object wrapped in a `Proxy` | `#` access does not go through the proxy)
claim_checks.page_says: they cannot be proxied, enumerated, deleted, or interacted with using any Object method.

claim_checks.claim: TypeScript downlevels it (row context: Target ES2021 or lower | `#` becomes `WeakMap` lookups)
claim_checks.page_says: When compiling to ES2021 or less, TypeScript will use WeakMaps in place of #.

claim_checks.claim: So code meant to run unbuilt keeps injected collaborators as `readonly #field`s assigned in the constructor (row context: Working around it with `--experimental-transform-types` | Runs on Node 24.22 with an `ExperimentalWarning` (re-tested 2026-11-03); the flag is removed in Node 26.0.0)
claim_checks.note: The cited page (Node v26.13.1 docs) supports only the v26.0.0 removal and that parameter properties need transformation. Searched 'ExperimentalWarning', '24.22', 'private', 'readonly': not found. The Node 24.22 behaviour is a local re-test that a v26 page cannot back, and the readonly #field recommendation is the doc's own inference.

claim_checks.claim: Node only deletes types (row context: Type stripping itself | Stable (stability 2) since Node 24.12.0 and 25.2.0; no warning since 24.3.0; Node ignores `tsconfig.json` and needs `.ts` extensions in relative imports)
claim_checks.page_says: Since Node.js is only removing inline types, any TypeScript features that involve replacing TypeScript syntax with new JavaScript syntax will error.
claim_checks.note: The context cell matches the page's History table (stable at v25.2.0 and v24.12.0; the experimental warning dropped at v24.3.0), its statement that tsconfig.json is ignored, and its rule that file extensions are mandatory in imports.

conflicts.topic: Runtime cost of hard-private (#) fields. The handbook warns that runtime privacy checks, private fields included, could affect performance. The V8 blog says V8 9.7 made initialization as fast as ordinary property assignment when the pattern is predictable. 'Could' is a hedge and the V8 result is engine-specific, so the two do not contradict each other, and the doc's ✅ claims C3 and C6 report each one in its own terms. The unmarked Summary line ('costs the same as public fields' on any native ES2022+ target) and the Takeaway ('measured cost is nil') go further than either source; see violations.

violations.evidence: C1: the handbook gives the bracket-notation escape hatch and the 'soft private' label for private only ('private also allows access using bracket notation during type checking'). The claim applies them to protected members as well.

C6: the V8 blog uses the new IC only 'when V8 considers the pattern of the initialization to be predictable enough' and falls back to a runtime call otherwise. The claim states the move to the fast path with no condition.

C9: the ✅[^4] row asserts Node 24.22 behaviour (an ExperimentalWarning, re-tested 2026-11-03) and a readonly #field recommendation, but the cited Node v26.13.1 page has neither. The References entry for [^4] also says it backs 'the 24.22.1 behaviour re-tested the same day', which is a local result, and that entry gives the version as 24.22.1 where the body says 24.22.

Factual claims in the Summary and in role 1-5 sections have neither a ✅ nor a ⚠️ mark: the Summary's 'reading and creating # fields costs the same as public fields' on any native ES2022+ target (the V8 blog covers initialization only, in V8 only); 'TypeScript error TS18009' in the role-3 'Where each form fits' table (not found in [^1]); and the Worked example's measurements, which name no local artifact. Verification status still reports 'Unverified: 0 claims'.

The run gives outputs (milliseconds, JSON and Object.keys results) but not the benchmark code or a path to it, so a reader cannot reproduce it. This is the one weak section and the reason diataxis_rigor is 4. Roles 2 and 5 have no section of their own; for a narrow concept doc of this type that was not counted as a missing role.
